question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, because the Generality Constraint requires that if one grasps Fa and also grasps the universal quantifier, one must be able to apply the same predicate uniformly to any object in the domain. There is no non-arbitrary point at which competence with substitution instances could stop once those two pieces are in place; otherwise the grasp of Fa would not be fully general. This holds even before one considers whether the resulting quantified sentence is true.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, because once the Generality Constraint is in place and we already grasp both Fa and the universal quantifier, the same open-sentence competence must extend uniformly across arbitrary substitution instances Fx; there is no principled cutoff that would let us stop short of full predicative coverage without violating the constraint. I'm roughly 70% confident on this reading.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Gareth Evans' Generality Constraint requires that if a thinker grasps the thought Fa, they must possess the conceptual resources to understand Fb for any object b in the relevant domain. Given that we are also assuming grasp of the universal quantifier ∀x, this appears to push strongly toward competence with the full open sentence Fx (i.e., the predicate F applied uniformly across the quantified domain). Without that, the constraint would seem to permit arbitrary gaps in substitution that lack any principled basis in the semantics of quantification itself. That said, Evans' own writings sometimes leave room for limited cognitive restrictions on very large or abstract domains, so I would put the probability at roughly 65% that the answer is yes under a strict reading.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint (GC), grasping Fa already requires that the thinker can entertain Fb for any object b they can think about (i.e., the predicate is understood as generally applicable across the thinker's singular thoughts). Given that universal quantification is independently understood, this recombinatorial capacity directly yields grasp of ∀x Fx, since the quantified proposition is composed out of the same predicate applied across the entire relevant domain of objects. GC does not by itself introduce quantificational concepts, but once those are granted, the transition from singular to universally quantified understanding follows.

(The notation "Fx (∀x)" is interpreted throughout as the closed sentence ∀x Fx.)

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. Evans' Generality Constraint requires only that grasp of Fa enables recombination of its constituents with other understood singular terms (yielding Fb, Fc, etc.) inside atomic thoughts of the same form. It does not extend to the distinct logical operation of binding a variable with a universal quantifier to produce ∀x Fx, even when the quantifier itself is already grasped.

(The GC secures systematicity and productivity within the Fregean “building-block” model of atomic thought; quantified propositions lie outside that model.)

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. Evans' Generality Constraint requires only that possession of the constituents of Fa enables recombination with any other singular concepts one grasps (e.g., Fb, Fc …). It does not impose any requirement to grasp quantified propositions such as ∀x Fx, even when the quantifier itself is understood. The latter involves an additional layer of generality over a domain, which lies outside the recombinatorial demand on singular thoughts.

(The question's parenthetical “∀x” is therefore not licensed by GC alone.)

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, Evans' Generality Constraint (GC) does not entail that grasp of Fa yields grasp of ∀x Fx (even given grasp of the quantifier). GC requires only that the constituent concepts be freely recombinable across singular thoughts: if a thinker can entertain Fa then, for any other object b they can think about, they can entertain Fb, and for any other property G they can think about, they can entertain Ga. Quantified propositions are not singular thoughts of this form; they require an additional apparatus of quantifier-variable binding that GC does not itself supply. Hence the constraint is satisfied without the ability to form or understand ∀x Fx.

(The question may be conflating the “generality” of GC with the generality expressed by quantifiers; these are distinct.)

It does not extend to the distinct cognitive capacity needed to bind a predicate into a genuinely quantified thought ∀x Fx, even when the quantifier itself is understood. The two abilities can therefore come apart.

(The constraint is silent on whether singular thought automatically yields mastery of generality over an entire domain.)
